items.stem: Which conditions are used in the industrial hydration of ethene to make ethanol?
options: steam with a phosphoric acid catalyst, about 300 °C and 6 MPa
hydrogen with a nickel catalyst at 150 °C
items.answer: steam with a phosphoric acid catalyst, about 300 °C and 6 MPa
items.markingKey: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃CH₂OH.

items.stem: Explain why sodium reacts less vigorously with ethanol than with water.
items.answer: The ethyl group pushes electrons towards O, so the O–H bond in ethanol is less polar and H⁺ is less readily released than from water.
items.markingKey: ethyl group electron-donating / O–H less polar [1]; H⁺ released less readily, slower reaction [1]

items.stem: Explain why the lower alcohols are soluble in water but the solubility falls as the chain gets longer.
items.answer: The –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water; longer hydrocarbon chains cannot hydrogen bond and disrupt water's hydrogen bonding, so solubility falls.
items.markingKey: OH hydrogen bonds with water [1]; longer non-polar chain reduces solubility [1]

items.stem: Lucas, a student in Lisbon, adds excess sodium to 1.85 g of propan-1-ol. Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³, produced at room temperature and pressure (molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹).
items.answer: 370 cm³

items.stem: Jonas, a student in Karachi, adds excess sodium to 2.30 g of propan-1-ol. Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³, produced at room temperature and pressure (molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹).
items.answer: 460 cm³

items.stem: A biofuel producer in Toronto makes butan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH, for blending with petrol. (a) Classify the alcohol and explain your answer. (b) Explain why it is miscible with water. (c) Suggest one environmental advantage of using it as a fuel.
items.answer: (a) primary: the C–OH carbon is bonded to one other carbon atom. (b) The –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules. (c) It can be made from renewable biomass, so it is closer to carbon neutral.
items.markingKey: (a) primary: the C–OH carbon is bonded to one other carbon atom. [2] (b) The –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules. [1] (c) It can be made from renewable biomass, so it is closer to carbon neutral. [1]

items.stem: What are the products when ethanol reacts with sodium?
items.answer: sodium ethoxide and hydrogen
items.markingKey: 2CH₃CH₂OH + 2Na → 2CH₃CH₂O⁻Na⁺ + H₂.

items.stem: Explain why ethanol is considered a useful fuel.
items.answer: It burns completely to CO₂ and H₂O releasing a lot of energy per mole, and it can be made from renewable plant material (fermentation), although land is used to grow the crops.
items.markingKey: exothermic combustion/clean products [1]; renewable source [1]

items.stem: In a test answer, Nadia states: "2-methylpropan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol because the –OH is on carbon 2." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. The C–OH carbon is attached to three other carbons, so it is tertiary.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Grace writes in a revision note: "Butan-2-ol is a primary alcohol because the –OH group is on the second carbon." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. The C–OH carbon is attached to two other carbon atoms, so butan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Kwame, a student in Cape Town, burns butan-1-ol in a spirit burner under a copper can containing 100 g of water. The mass of the burner decreases by 0.55 g and the temperature of the water rises by 28.5 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of butan-1-ol (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).
items.answer: −1600 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Give the reagents and conditions for making 2-methylpropan-2-ol from 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, and write an equation for the reaction.
items.answer: NaOH(aq), warm; (CH₃)₃CBr + NaOH → (CH₃)₃COH + NaBr
items.markingKey: NaOH(aq), warm [1]; (CH₃)₃CBr + NaOH → (CH₃)₃COH + NaBr [1]

items.stem: Mohammed, a student in Auckland, adds excess sodium to 0.92 g of ethanol. Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³, produced at room temperature and pressure (molar gas volume 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹). Name the organic product.
items.answer: 240 cm³; sodium ethoxide, CH₃CH₂O⁻Na⁺
items.markingKey: 2ROH + 2Na → 2RONa + H₂ [1]; n(ethanol) = 0.92/46.0 = 0.0200 mol [1]; n(H₂) = 0.0100 mol, V = 240 cm³ [1]; sodium ethoxide [1]

items.stem: Mohammed studies methanol, CH₃OH, in a quality-control laboratory. (a) Classify the alcohol and explain your answer. (b) Write an equation for its complete combustion.
items.answer: (a) primary: the C–OH carbon is bonded to no other carbon atom (methanol is treated as primary). (b) CH₄O + 1½O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
items.markingKey: (a) primary: the C–OH carbon is bonded to no other carbon atom (methanol is treated as primary). [2] (b) CH₄O + 1½O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O [1]

What colour change is seen when propan-2-ol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
items.answer: orange to green
items.markingKey: Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) is reduced to Cr³⁺ (green).

items.stem: Explain why tertiary alcohols resist oxidation by acidified dichromate(VI).
items.answer: The carbon bearing –OH has no hydrogen atom, so it cannot form C=O without breaking a C–C bond.
items.markingKey: no H on the C–OH carbon [1]; C=O cannot form without breaking C–C [1]

items.stem: Explain why heating under reflux leads to a carboxylic acid from a primary alcohol.
items.answer: Reflux returns the volatile aldehyde to the flask, so it stays in contact with excess oxidising agent and is oxidised further to the acid.
items.markingKey: vapours condense and return [1]; aldehyde further oxidised by excess oxidant [1]

items.stem: Omar, a student in Singapore, warms propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Describe what is observed and give the organic product(s) formed, with equations.

items.markingKey: orange → green [1]; propanone [1]; CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + [O] → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O [1]

items.answer: (a) 2-methylpropan-2-ol: tertiary; propan-2-ol: secondary (b) Aldehydes give a red-brown precipitate with warm Fehling's solution (or a silver mirror with Tollens'); ketones do not; a tertiary alcohol gives no product.

items.stem: Explain why dehydration of butan-2-ol gives more than one alkene.
items.answer: Water can be lost with an H from C1 or C3, giving but-1-ene or but-2-ene; but-2-ene has cis and trans isomers, giving three alkenes.
items.markingKey: H removed from either neighbouring carbon [1]; cis/trans but-2-ene [1]

items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: What is the catalyst in the esterification of ethanoic acid with ethanol?
items.answer: concentrated sulfuric acid
items.markingKey: A few drops of conc H₂SO₄; the mixture is heated.

items.stem: Explain why esters have lower boiling points than carboxylic acids of similar Mr.
items.answer: Ester molecules have no O–H group, so they cannot hydrogen bond to each other; carboxylic acids form hydrogen bonds (dimers).
items.markingKey: no H bonding between ester molecules [1]; acids hydrogen bond [1]

items.stem: Explain why alkaline hydrolysis of an ester goes to completion but acid hydrolysis does not.
items.answer: In alkali the carboxylic acid is converted to a carboxylate ion, which cannot react with the alcohol, so the reverse reaction is removed; acid hydrolysis is a reversible equilibrium.
items.markingKey: carboxylate ion formed / does not react with alcohol [1]; acid hydrolysis reversible [1]

items.answer: (a) butanoic acid and propan-1-ol; concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst, heat under reflux (b) CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH + CH₃CH₂CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃CH₂CH₂COOCH₂CH₂CH₃ + H₂O (c) sodium butanoate and propan-1-ol

items.stem: Explain why esterification is carried out with heating under reflux and concentrated sulfuric acid.
items.answer: Reaction is slow: heat increases rate, reflux prevents loss of volatile reactants and products, and H₂SO₄ catalyses the reaction (and absorbs water, shifting the equilibrium right).
items.markingKey: reflux keeps volatiles / heat increases rate [1]; catalyst (and dehydrating agent) [1]

items.stem: A perfume chemist in Mumbai uses oxidation and dehydration of alcohols. Explain why heating under reflux leads to a carboxylic acid from a primary alcohol.
items.answer: Reflux returns the volatile aldehyde to the flask, so it stays in contact with excess oxidising agent and is oxidised further to the acid.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the lower alcohols are soluble in water but the solubility falls as the chain gets longer. (b) Explain why sodium reacts less vigorously with ethanol than with water.
items.answer: (a) The –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water; longer hydrocarbon chains cannot hydrogen bond and disrupt water's hydrogen bonding, so solubility falls. (b) The ethyl group pushes electrons towards O, so the O–H bond in ethanol is less polar and H⁺ is less readily released than from water.
items.markingKey: (a) OH hydrogen bonds with water [1]; longer non-polar chain reduces solubility [1] (b) ethyl group electron-donating / O–H less polar [1]; H⁺ released less readily, slower reaction [1]

items.stem: A perfume chemist in Hanoi uses oxidation and dehydration of alcohols. Explain why tertiary alcohols resist oxidation by acidified dichromate(VI).

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why heating under reflux leads to a carboxylic acid from a primary alcohol. (b) Explain why dehydration of butan-2-ol gives more than one alkene.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why esterification is carried out with heating under reflux and concentrated sulfuric acid. (b) Explain why esters have lower boiling points than carboxylic acids of similar Mr.
items.answer: (a) Reaction is slow: heat increases rate, reflux prevents loss of volatile reactants and products, and H₂SO₄ catalyses the reaction (and absorbs water, shifting the equilibrium right).
